summary: Marks outlines Oaktree's philosophy: risk control first, no macro forecasting or market timing, target less efficient markets, understand cycles and act only at sentiment extremes. Market valuation was somewhat above fair value in mid-2024 but not extreme. Contrarian betting needs payoff-over-probability thinking, temperature-taking and tolerance of looking wrong.

coverage.note: intro; Oaktree's six-point philosophy, no macro forecasting, market efficiency
limits of knowledge, randomness, decision quality, cycles

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: it's easy to make money in the market that's especially true in the good years and most years are good years
claims.claim: The real skill is making money with risk under control so a bad year does not do much damage; the goal is consistency slightly above the middle with bounce to the top in bad years.
claims.testable: partly: judged by drawdown and relative rank

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: I believe there's such a thing as market efficiency and we Target only the less efficient markets
claims.claim: Target less efficient markets (credit, niches) because in efficient markets one cannot know more than others; specialization in a few things is required.

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: we don't rely on macro forecasting to drive our investments and number six we don't uh expect much from Market timing
claims.claim: Oaktree does not rely on macro forecasting or market timing, because forecasters are not right consistently enough to follow.
claims.testable: partly: forecaster hit rates can be tracked

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: an economist is a portfolio manager who never marks the market
claims.claim: Economists, unlike active managers, never show a track record, so their forecasts should not be hired or followed without one.
claims.testable: yes: track records can be requested and scored

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: you're dealing with in large part people I mean what are markets it's a collection of people
claims.claim: Markets are made of people with feelings, so processes cannot be predicted like physical laws and randomness plays a very large role.

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: you can't tell the quality of a decision from the outcome
claims.claim: Because of randomness, a good decision can fail and a bad one can succeed, so judge decisions by process, not result; in the short run randomness can produce almost any outcome.

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: the ingredients in success are aggressiveness timing and skill and if you have enough aggressiveness at the right time you don't need much skill
claims.claim: Success can come from aggression at the right time without skill, which can make one right once or twice; only repeated success over a career demonstrates skill.

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: nothing moves in a straight line uh where human behavior is involved and if you were to count on it doing so you would uh get into big trouble
claims.claim: The economy, markets and politics move cyclically, and extrapolating a straight line gets investors in trouble.

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: regression toward the mean or the correction uh of uh excesses is much more dependable than continued moving in a straight line
claims.claim: The biggest investor mistake is assuming a market moving in one direction will continue; reversion of excess is more dependable than continuation.

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: the answer is that people go to excess and for example if the economy is growing well for a few years business uh heads say oh well we have to build a new Factory
claims.claim: Cycles arise because people overreact: good growth leads firms to overbuild capacity, utilization falls, firms pull back (greed and fear pendulum).

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: when the market is crazy high or crazy low I think we can uh make a profitable uh forecast
claims.claim: Forecasting is useful only at extremes, when a bubble or crash is likely to revert, but such opportunities are rare.
claims.indicator: market extremes in valuation and sentiment
claims.conditions: only at crazy highs or lows

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: five times in 50 years five times the market has been at such an extreme that regression toward the mean has been dependable
claims.claim: Marks' contrarian market forecasts were possible only five times in 50 years, and reversion was dependable in direction but not in timing, cause or speed.
claims.testable: yes: number of episodes is small

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: I think we're a little bit above uh fair value but not so high that a decline is uh predictable or Dependable
claims.claim: In mid-2024 the US stock market was somewhat above fair value, not at an extreme that makes a decline dependable.

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: we get a reading in the stock market every day we don't get frequent readings in the credit market and in private credit we never get readings
claims.claim: The S&P 500 is used as a daily barometer of investor psychology because credit and private credit are priced infrequently.

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: if you name a price don't name a date if you name a date don't name a price
claims.claim: A forecaster should name a price or a date, not both, since valuation signals have unreliable timing.

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: the PE Ratio is 21 the post-war Norm is 16 so 20 25% overvalued
claims.claim: The S&P 500 PE of 21 versus a post-war norm of 16 implies about 20-25% overvaluation.
claims.testable: yes: PE and long-run average observable

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: it's probably a little better than 50/50 but it's not 100 or 90
claims.claim: Even if the market is overvalued, the probability of a decline in the next year is only a little better than 50/50, because overpriced markets often become more overpriced before a bubble.

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: most bubbles do surround something that's new and this one does
claims.claim: Bubbles typically form around something new that impresses everyone, and AI stocks may be one, though Marks admits he does not know.

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: it's okay to have an opinion on these subjects it's just not okay to bet the client's money
claims.claim: An opinion on areas one does not know well (China cheap, AI) is fine but should not be bet with client money.

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: risk avoidance usually results in return avoidance
claims.claim: Sound risk management is not risk avoidance; take risk that is aware, analyzable, diversifiable and highly paid.
claims.conditions: risk must be understood, analyzable, diversifiable, and well paid

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: China has been marked down by everybody many people describe it as uninvestable
claims.claim: China may be too cheap after being marked down and called uninvestable, but Marks does not know enough to say.

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: risk means more things can happen than will happen
claims.claim: Under any circumstance a variety of outcomes is possible, so allow for the vagaries of the future; excessive certainty is the enemy.

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: there was a high Dee degree of consensus that the FED would cut rat six times this year
claims.claim: In December 2023 the consensus of six Fed cuts in 2024 was excessively optimistic 'Goldilocks thinking'; expectations later fell to two or three.

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: it's kind of like calculus and the second uh derivative
claims.claim: Optimism fell at the margin (fewer cuts expected) but optimists still govern the market, which stalled but did not decline.

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: I think it's everybody's job to control risk and the the person who advocates for a given investment and studies it should be the person who not only thinks about the return but also the risk
claims.claim: No separate risk department; the investment advocate owns risk, so nobody can count on others to limit risk.

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: the proper fixed income investor uh has to think about and avoid the downside doesn't have to worry about the upside
claims.claim: Fixed income has capped upside, so the skill is avoiding losers (Graham and Dodd: negative art).

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: negative rates were not a market phenomenon they were uh administered by the central banks
claims.claim: Negative rates were administered by central banks, unsustainable in Marks' view, but in the short run don't fight the Fed.

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: what sense does it make for Market participants to say there will be six Cuts If the Fed itself is saying there will be three
claims.claim: Market pricing of six cuts versus the Fed dot plot of three was a mistake from excess optimism.
claims.indicator: fed funds futures vs dot plot

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: avoiding the losers is not enough in that case you have to actually find some winners
claims.claim: Avoiding losers works for 8% fixed income targets but aspirational 15-20% targets also require finding winners.

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: assessing probabilities is very very important uh structuring your bet knowing when you have an advantage
claims.claim: Games teach probabilistic thinking, risk-taking, structuring bets and knowing when you hold an edge, which carries over to investing.

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: it's not what outcome is likely to happen but it's is the payoff better for investing in the team that will probably win sometimes the payoff is better for investing in the team that will probably lose
claims.claim: Betting requires comparing payoff with probability, so the underdog can be the better investment; this is thinking in bets.

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: knowledge consensus is already embodied in the price of every asset
claims.claim: Because consensus is in the price, you can only make money by finding where the consensus is wrong and the payoff to the unlikely outcome is high.

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: I don't think it's a good idea to routinely say well what does the consensus think let's do the opposite
claims.claim: Contrarianism is not mechanical; ask what the consensus thinks, what is wrong with it, and what could expose the error.

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: you don't usually make much money by betting on the thing that everybody else loves the big money is made by betting on the things they hate which as a result are cheap
claims.claim: Big money comes from buying what everyone hates because it is cheap, not from buying what everyone loves.

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: you have to dare to look wrong because even if you're right that's probably not going to be clear for some time
claims.claim: Exceptional investing requires being different, wrong and looking wrong for a period, so partners and a supporting structure matter.

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: we were very steady buyers in the 15 weeks following the bankruptcy of Leman Brothers 650 million a week on average for 15 weeks that's $10 billion
claims.claim: After Lehman, Oaktree bought steadily about $650m a week for 15 weeks, with a partner's support; contrarian action gets easier with a trusted partner and experience.
claims.direction: buy distressed credit steadily in crisis

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: I just look at what opinions are being expressed how uniformly are they held how strongly are they held how self-satisfied are the people who are holding them
claims.claim: Marks takes the market temperature by checking how uniform, strong and self-satisfied the opinions are.
claims.testable: partly: could be proxied by survey dispersion

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: I think it's easier when the markets are frothy
claims.claim: Being contrarian is easier in frothy markets than fearful ones, though froth is hard to measure.

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: silliest of reasons their justifications just don't hold and so hopefully you can see through that and and get off the train
claims.claim: In the 2000 internet bubble those making the most money held opinions with silly justifications, which one can see through and exit before the cliff.

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: people say that they this is they're the most uncertain they've ever been in my book that's healthy
claims.claim: Widespread admission of uncertainty means the market temperature is moderate, since certainty is dangerous.

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: he says the enemy of knowledge is not ignorance it's the illusion of knowledge
claims.claim: The illusion of knowledge stops inquiry, so acknowledging not knowing is healthy.

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: everybody has the data everybody knows what's happening in the world today and what happened yesterday to me the most important thing is to sit and say what does it mean
claims.claim: Edge comes from interpreting data and judging where we stand in the cycle, not from having data.

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: the markets were acting in a Carefree nonrisk conscious manner which to me is the most dangerous thing
claims.claim: Marks was worried before the GFC without knowing subprime existed, because markets behaved in a carefree, non risk-conscious way; contrarian stands are not data-driven.

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: you can't be an investor satisfactorily if you have to be right all the time
claims.claim: Because of randomness an investor cannot be right every time (unlike a dentist), so one must be able to stand being wrong.

claims.speaker: Howard Marks
claims.quote: if you're right 60% or 70% of the time you you'll be the smartest man in the world
claims.claim: A hit rate of 60-70% makes an investor exceptional, so do not require infallibility.
